newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Euro-MPs row over lead in drinking water.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MPs row over lead in drinking water.

text.p: A fierce row between Euro-MPs over the best way to cut the amount of poisonous lead in drinking water threatens to burst into the open on December 11.

At issue is whether European Union countries should be forced to replace lead pipes with plastic ones, at an estimated cost of over 35 billion Ecus, or whether an equally effective but cheaper alternative can be found.

Next Wednesday the European Parliament is due to examine a European Commission proposal to tighten up a 1980 EU directive on the quality of drinking water, namely by making an 80 percent cut in the permitted lead content.

In its proposal -- COM(94)612 -- the Commission follows the line adopted by the World Health Organisation in recommending a cut in the maximum allowed lead content from 50 miligrammes per litre to 10mg/l.

The Commission believes the member states should have 15 years to meet this target, which will entail replacing miles and miles of old lead pipes, particularly in Belgium, Britain, France, Spain, Portugal and Italy.
But a report approved last month by parliament's environment committee insists the member states should be made to clean up their act within 10 years.

According to the report, drafted by committee chairman Ken Collins, the member states' record of compliance with the existing directive is so dismal that the EU should keep intense pressure on them to take action.
"It is a realistic proposal. The member states can do it," an assistant to Collins told Reuters on Thursday.
"They should have been working on these measures over the last 16 years under the present directive," he pointed out.
But the line of action advocated by the British Socialist is not supported by all members of the environment committee.

French Christian Democrat Francoise Grossetete argues that cutting the lead in water to 10mg/l is not feasible, given the astronomical cost of replacing lead pipes, and unjustifiable because the WHO's research is inconclusive.

Instead, Grossetete advocates cutting the lead content by only 50 percent (to 25mg/l), which could be done by chemically treating the water, while forcing the member states to comply within the shorter time of five years.
"We know lead is dangerous to health but we don't know if bringing the limit down to 10 miligrammes will help," the Euro- MP's assistant Geraldine Philibert told Reuters.

"The WTO studies are based on an extreme case -- the effect of lead on babies at bottle feeding age," she continued, adding that Grossetete thought more research was needed to find out the effect of different lead limits on the less-vulnerable majority of the population.

The Euro-MP was also concerned about the lack of research into the long-term effects of replacement plastic pipes on human health, when plastic was known to provoke endocrinial disorders, Philibert said.
She added that young babies, who the WTO says are vulnerable to anything over 0.1 mg of lead, could be protected by giving them only bottled water.
"No doctor would recommend making up a bottle with tap water," she said.
Grossetete's alternative amendment to the draft directive is backed by the 57-member Union for Europe group but has not won unqualified support from her own 182-member European People's Party.
German EPP members were not backing Grossetete, Philibert said.
"They are not very concerned. Germany has very little lead piping. It uses plastic."
The drinking water proposal is one of two analyses of water policy which the parliament will consider under the cooperation procedure at next week's plenary session.
The other, a report on a Commission proposal to clean up Europe's bathing waters -- COM(94)36 -- is also controversial.
Rapporteur Doeke Eisma is recommending widening the scope of the new law to cover waters used for all watersports, not just bathing, in a move which has upset some British Euro-MPs.
"It would apply to all waters around Britain," British Conservative Caroline Jackson protested.
She said she had persuaded the EPP to vote against Eisma's amendment.
The two proposals are "daughter directives" to a planned framework directive on the EU's overall water policy, which the Parliament approved in October.
